Host/Network Artifacts: Non-machine account (not ending in $) performing DS-Replication-Get-Changes operations on the domain root; network traffic to DC on RPC/TCP 135 and high ephemeral ports from a non-DC IP; no physical file artifacts on DC (memory-resident attack)
Logic: Non-DC Account Replication Rights: DCSync abuses the DRSGetNCChanges RPC interface to request password hashes from a DC by impersonating a replication partner. The DC validates only whether the requesting account has Replicating Directory Changes extended rights - not whether it is a real DC. Event 4662 captures this operation. The critical filter is SubjectUserName not ending in $ (machine accounts): legitimate DC-to-DC replication always originates from computer accounts. A human or service account performing replication is the definitive anomaly. IMPORTANT: This detection requires manual enablement of DS Access auditing under Advanced Audit Policy Configuration - it is NOT active by default. GUIDs: {1131f6aa} = Replicating Directory Changes; {1131f6ad} = Replicating Directory Changes All. NOTE: Machine account filter alone is insufficient - non-DC machine accounts (e.g. WS01$) can also be granted replication rights. Pair with a DC hostname whitelist for higher fidelity.
Common False Positives: Azure AD Connect sync accounts; legitimate backup solutions (Veeam; Commvault); third-party IdP connectors; non-DC machine accounts that have been granted replication rights _ these are themselves a misconfiguration worth investigating

Unlike Mimikatz PTH, Rubeus sends this AS-REQ directly to DC port 88 without routing through lsass.exe. This generates a legitimate-looking EventID 4768 on the DC, defeating the transaction-based PtT detection. Common False Positives: Same false positive profile as Rubeus PtT detection above; any non-standard Kerberos client implementation

Detection window is narrow: Mimikatz automatically unregisters the rogue DC after replication completes. Real-time alerting is essential.
